https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.text: By Thomas Copeland BBC Verify Published 15 September 2026 Satellite imagery shows a key oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia has been badly damaged after a strike last week, which experts have told BBC Verify could take more than a month to repair and force oil prices even higher. The image shows the most significant damage is at a pumping station along the East-West Pipeline, which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on to export crude oil via the Red Sea rather than through the Strait of Hormuz, where ships have been attacked by Iran and the US during their six-month war. The Saudi government has accused Iranian-backed militias in Iraq of the pipeline strike, which followed days of renewed missile and drone attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthi group - which is also backed by Iran. Saudi Arabia has retaliated by carrying out strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of western Yemen. New satellite images also show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base after a Houthi strike last week. The Saudi government said on Tuesday it would respond "firmly" to attacks by the Houthis. While the Houthis have been fighting a long-running civil war against Saudi-backed Yemeni pro-government forces, the group has stepped up its campaign in recent weeks. It seized control of significant new territory across Yemen's south-western coast last week, including areas overlooking the crucial Bab al-Mandab waterway, strengthening its ability to enforce its declared blockade of Saudi shipping. The price of a barrel of oil has surged since Saudi Arabia said on Friday it was closing the pipeline as a precaution. Brent crude was trading as high as $108 (Â£80) a barrel on Tuesday, down slightly from $109.80 on Monday. Experts from trade intelligence firm Kpler said the pipeline's closure could reduce oil supplies by as much as 3.6 million barrels per day - or about 3.6% of global demand. "Based on new information we've received, damage to the pipeline could take four to six weeks to resolve, given spare-parts availability and impaired supply chains," said Homayoun Falakshahi, Kpler's head of crude oil analysis. Anne-Sophie Corbeau, from the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University, said pipelines are "like sitting ducks" and recent strikes are a "very important signal" indicating workarounds being used to avoid the Strait of Hormuz "may not be super useful because they can be destroyed". The Houthis have targeted other Saudi oil infrastructure with drones and missiles which has led to some operations being suspended. There have also been attacks on military bases. New satellite images captured on Monday show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base near Khamis Mushait which the Houthis said they had targeted with ballistic missiles and drones last week after it was used to carry out air strikes on Yemen. At least three aircraft hangars or shelters appear to have been damaged at the Royal Saudi Air Force facility where US-made F-15 fighter jets are based. The Saudi-led anti-Houthi military coalition of Arab states said on Tuesday that a Houthi missile and drone attack had injured 13 people in attacks on what the coalition said were "civilian objects". The Houthis said Saudi Arabia had carried out with more than 50 strikes in western Yemen over the previous 24 hours. The UN Refugee Agency has said that more than 100,000 people have been internally displaced by the renewed conflict. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Perth siblings Jake and Callum Robinson, 30 and 33. The three men found guilty of their murders have been sentenced to 158 years in prison each. Photograph: SUPPLIED/PR IMAGE View image in fullscreen Perth siblings Jake and Callum Robinson, 30 and 33. The three men found guilty of their murders have been sentenced to 158 years in prison each. Photograph: SUPPLIED/PR IMAGE Mexico Mexican judge sentences three men to 158 years in prison for murders of Australian and US surfers​ Australian ​brothers Jake ​and Callum Robinson, and ​their ‌American friend Carter Rhoad, were killed while on a surf trip in Baja California in 2024 Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Kat Wong with agencies Fri 16 Oct 2026 22.52 EDT Last modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 00.11 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Mexican ⁠judge ⁠has sentenced ​three men to 158 years ⁠and nine months in prison each for ⁠the murder of ​two Australian ‌brothers ‌and their American friend during ‌a 2024 surf trip to the state of Baja California. The ‌defendants were declared guilty a week ​ago of homicide, aggravated robbery, robbery with violence and vehicle theft ⁠with violence, crimes committed against ​Australian ​brothers Jake ​and Callum Robinson, and ​their ‌American friend ​Carter Rhoad. Rhoad and the Robinsons were shot dead in a suspected robbery while travelling through Mexico . They were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked on 27 April 2024. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Their bodies were found days later in a clifftop well with gunshot wounds to the heads. Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons. Two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were also found guilty and have been sentenced. The families of the victims followed the sentencing hearing via video link. View image in fullscreen Debra and Martin Robinson, parents of Australian brothers Callum and Jake Robinson, during a news conference outside court after the verdict. Photograph: Karen Castaneda/AP Prosecutors had requested damages of more than $100,000 but the judge ruled against it and said any compensation would have to be pursued through civil proceedings. The brothers’ parents, Martin and Debra Robinson, travelled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September. They have established a foundation in their sons’ names to carry on their legacy. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion The Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation aims to “help people live bigger, shine brighter and love harder in their honour”. Callum, the older of the two brothers, moved to the US as a professional lacrosse player and has been remembered for his loving nature and passion for the environment, having been involved in coastal cleanups. Jake, a doctor, was set to take up a position at Geelong hospital after returning to Australia. He has been remembered for his academic success, his passion for sport, particularly cricket and surfing, and his compassion. Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast. Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while travelling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned. Photograph: ARSVOM/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The Wine Trader ship was struck in the territorial waters of Romania, near Sulina, on Thursday. Photograph: ARSVOM/AFP/Getty Images Shipping industry Intensifying drone attacks on ships in Black Sea bring war ever closer to Nato shores Six attacks in 10 days by suspected Russian drones mark dramatic escalation in maritime conflict Peter Beaumont Senior international correspondent Sun 18 Oct 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 01.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T he first the crew of the Bulgarian ferry Dioscuria knew of an attack on a cargo ship in their country’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea in the early hours of 6 October was a distant explosion 70 miles off the coastal town of Byala. The Turkish-owned Alfa Watan, heading for the Romanian port of Sulina, had been struck by suspected Russian air and naval drones. Arriving on the scene, Dioscuria found an overturned lifeboat and lifejackets in the water. There was no sign, however, of Alfa Watan’s crew of 10. Map showing location of ships attacked in the Black Sea’s EU waters in October Six days later drones struck another ship off the coast of Bulgaria, HS Dignity. Eleven crew members died. By Thursday, the attacks had encroached on Romania’s airspace and territorial water. Two chemical tankers, Wine Trader and Yara J, were attacked and left burning. Seven more sailors were missing. View image in fullscreen Four of the rescued sailors from HS Dignity on a Bulgarian navy rescue tug, which transported them to the port of Varna on Tuesday. Photograph: moreto.net/AP View image in fullscreen Crew members from the Able, which was damaged in a drone attack, disembark from a Bulgarian border police vessel in Varna after a rescue operation. Photograph: Petko Momchilov/Reuters The attacks on six ships in 10 days – the Able and Chelsea-3 were also hit – marked a dramatic escalation in a maritime conflict that is pressing on Nato’s borders. While global attention has focused on the risks for sailors travelling through the strait of Hormuz, in recent months it is the Black Sea that has emerged as the more dangerous passage, with more sailors lost in a week and a half than US service members killed in the entire Iran war. View image in fullscreen Alfa Watan, which sank after a drone attack, sails in Istanbul, Turkey, the day before the incident. Photograph: Yoruk Isik/Reuters The maritime insurer and risk analyst Ambrey has warned that there is no end in sight to the threats to Black Sea cargo shipping, including grain and oil, and that insurance prices for passage of the waters have rocketed. Tomas Alexa, a senior analyst at Ambrey, has noted a sharp increase in the tempo of attacks beginning in July. Russian forces are estimated to be responsible for 80% of them. The recent loss of life, he suggests, has been exacerbated by “double tap” attacks involving aerial and surface drones, the latter often carrying up to half a tonne of explosive payloads. Smaller vessels that primarily use the Danube canal system have sunk rapidly. “While attacks against merchant vessels in the Black Sea are not new, we are seeing an escalation both in terms of the number of attacks and in the geographical scope,” Alexa said. The profile of vessels being attacked – that is, ships trading with Ukraine – had not changed, he added. “The Russian intent is clear, which is to degrade the export of Ukrainian grain and agricultural products.” View image in fullscreen The Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker Yara J transits the Bosphorus strait in Istanbul, Turkey, last month. Photograph: Yoruk Isik/Reuters The result has been a precipitous fall in the number of vessels visiting Ukraine. Insurance rates have soared, and seafarers and operators have become increasingly reluctant to operate in the Black Sea basin, even on ships unconnected with Ukrainian cargoes. The vast majority of the more than 60 fatalities of seafarers in the Black Sea since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 have occurred in the past year. In September the Joint War Committee, representing the London insurance market, moved to extend the high-risk areas of the Black Sea to include the whole of the basin, excluding the territorial waters of Turkey, Romania, Bulgaria and Georgia. The threat is not confined to the Black Sea itself. Attacks on Ukraine’s Black Sea ports have also increased sharply in the past year. A number of factors are driving the expansion and escalation of the conflict towards the shores of Nato countries, say experts. Russia has responded to a geographical expansion of Ukrainian strikes on its shadow fleet of oil tankers by intensifying strikes on Ukrainian agricultural cargoes – a key component of Kyiv’s economy. As ships sought safer passage further from the coastlines, so the threat has changed: from naval mines to drones, with ever longer ranges. Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, said after the sinking of the Alfa Watan: “Commercial ships – and innocent ​crews – are being targeted, ​with lives already lost at sea.” View image in fullscreen Demonstrators gather in Sofia, Bulgaria, on Thursday during a protest demanding clarification over recent Black Sea maritime attacks. Photograph: Hristo Vladev/Anadolu/Getty Images In a statement at the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, Col Joby Rimmer, a senior British military adviser, said: “Attacks that fail to distinguish between military objectives and civilian vessels, or that are expected to cause excessive incidental harm to civilians and civilian vessels in relation to the anticipated military advantage, may violate international humanitarian law and the UN convention on the law of the sea. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion “Each attack raises the risk to crews of every nationality, drives up insurance costs and restricts the flow of food to those who depend on it. The UK is deeply concerned by the far-reaching consequences of successive crises across the global maritime domain. Stable and secure sea lanes are a global common good from which we all benefit.” Operators have warned of the wider impact on trade in the Black Sea, including from Bulgarian ports. In a recent interview on Bulgarian television, the shipping agency owner Todor Georgiev warned the Black Sea was in danger of becoming a “dead zone”. View image in fullscreen A vessel that was hit by a drone in the Black Sea this week. Photograph: Bulgarian Interior Ministry/Reuters “Whenever the Russians are caught having struck a ship with one of their drones, they claim the vessel was carrying weapons,” he said. “Weapons are not being transported to Ukraine via the Black Sea.” Rumen Radev, Bulgaria’s prime minister, has described the attacks in the vicinity of his country’s territorial waters as “absolutely unacceptable”. Bulgarian officials are calling for the EU and Nato to support the efforts to enhance security, while working with Turkey and Romania on increased regional security. Although they have refused to attribute blame to Russia, officials have said there is “no logic” for Ukraine to attack its own shipments. View image in fullscreen A cargo ship in the Black Sea on Thursday. Photograph: Nikolay Doychinov/AFP/Getty Images “We do not have clear and conclusive evidence to attribute responsibility to either side,” said Radev. “However, as I have already stated, the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation.” As Russian strikes on shipping move ever closer to the borders of Nato members, they pose mounting security challenges to the mutual defence organisation, which is already confronting Moscow’s growing hybrid warfare across Europe. There is speculation that the affected Nato countries may be forced to invoke article 4 of the organisation’s treaty, a step below the article 5 invocation of mutual self defence. Triggered twice already around the Ukraine war – in the immediate aftermath of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and by Poland in 2025 after Russian drones violated Warsaw’s airspace – it calls for formal crisis discussions on a security threat. On Thursday Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, met Radev and Nicușor ⁠Dan, Romania’s president, to ​discuss ‌security ‌in the Black Sea. Rutte said: “Nato ​will continue to work closely with ⁠our allies in ​the Black Sea, ​adjusting ​our deterrence ​and ‌defence ​posture ​as needed.” Another consequence of the escalating attacks is the renewed danger of a global food crisis. Ukraine and Russia are major exporters of grain, as is Romania. View image in fullscreen Diners at a restaurant overlooking the harbour in Varna. Photograph: Nikolay Doychinov/AFP/Getty Images “We’re looking ​at the Black Sea as a global food ​artery,” said Oana Toiu, the Romanian foreign minister, at a security ​conference in Warsaw last week. “It is currently, unfortunately, the deadliest sea when it comes to the number of casualties of sailors ​in the last months. That means ‌we need to increase our ​investments in deterrence, defence.” Damien Chevallier, the director of maritime safety at the UN’s International Maritime Organization, warned last month of the long-term impact on shipping caused by attacks linked to the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East. “With rising casualties across the Black Sea, Red Sea and strait of Hormuz, being a seafarer has become a genuinely dangerous profession,” he said. “Seafarers are not trained to deal with threats from actions which are linked to wider security issues or geopolitical situations. “What makes this moment genuinely unprecedented is not just the number of incidents, but the pattern behind them. Shipping has become a deliberate instrument of geopolitical leverage.” Explore more on these topics Shipping industry Water transport Drones (military) Ukraine Europe Nato Romania features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
